query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive approach that incorporates configurational disorder and phase-diagram–inspired parameters (e.g., from binary phase diagrams and dynamic amorphization models) can effectively identify high-entropy alloys with low phonon thermal conductivity, because the same microstructural features (such as amorphous or ultra-nanocrystalline near‐surface layers) that reduce shear strength and wear also enhance phonon scattering.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, disordered high-entropy alloys synthesized to have high configurational entropy and a uniform solid solution structure.
generation.intervention: Apply the predictive algorithm—which uses parameters derived from binary phase diagrams and first-principles–informed models—to screen and select HEA compositions anticipated to develop nanostructural features (e.g., dynamic amorphization leading to a near-surface amorphous layer) that enhance phonon scattering.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted at ambient temperature under controlled synthesis conditions ensuring formation of the single-phase disordered microstructure. The approach applies only if the alloy does not decompose into intermetallic phases.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous near-surface layer and a high density of grain boundaries that disrupt phonon propagation.
generation.mechanism: The disordered microstructure and associated grain-boundary effects dramatically shorten the phonon mean free path, thereby reducing phonon thermal conductivity compared to predictions made using more conventional ab initio or crystallographic models.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEAs selected by the predictive approach will demonstrate significantly lower phonon thermal conductivity—potentially an improvement in predictive accuracy of around 15–20% relative to traditional methods—and exhibit microstructural signatures (e.g., amorphous near-surface layers) that correlate with high phonon scattering.
generation.baseline: Current predictive approaches that rely solely on ab initio calculations or crystallographic descriptors without incorporating phase-diagram–inspired parameters and disorder-related mechanisms.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable primarily to single-phase, highly disordered HEAs. It may not hold in systems where phase separation, intermetallic formation, or other ordered microstructures dominate, or under conditions significantly different from ambient temperature and pressure.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism linking disordered microstructures to phonon scattering is supported by analogous observations in mechanical properties, the exact magnitude of improvement (e.g., the 15–20% figure) remains uncertain and is expected to vary with composition and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of high-entropy alloys that are predicted by the algorithm to show low phonon thermal conductivity and a comparable series of control alloys selected by traditional predictive methods. Characterize their microstructure using advanced TEM/STEM techniques to confirm the presence or absence of amorphous or ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layers. Use time-domain thermoreflectance or another reliable technique to measure phonon thermal conductivity.
measurements: Microstructure characterization (e.g., TEM/STEM imaging) to detect amorphous/ultra-nanocrystalline layers
Thermal conductivity measurements using time-domain thermoreflectance or similar method
Comparison of predicted versus measured thermal conductivity values
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEAs selected using the predictive algorithm do not consistently exhibit the targeted microstructural features or if their measured phonon thermal conductivity is not significantly (≈15–20% or more) lower than those predicted by conventional models (or than that of control samples), then the hypothesis is falsified.

High Entropy Alloys Mined From Binary Phase Diagrams

Abstract: High entropy alloys (HEA) are a new type of high-performance structural material. Their vast degrees of compositional freedom provide for extensive opportunities to design alloys with tailored properties. However, compositional complexities present challenges for alloy design. Current approaches have shown limited reliability in accounting for the compositional regions of single solid solution and composite phases. For the first time, a phenomenological method analysing binary phase diagrams to predict HEA phases is presented. The hypothesis is that the HEA structural stability is encoded within the phase diagrams. Accordingly, we introduce several phase-diagram inspired parameters and employ machine learning (ML) to classify 600+ reported HEAs based on these parameters. Compared to other large database statistical prediction models, this model gives more detailed and accurate phase predictions. Both the overall HEA prediction and specifically single-phase HEA prediction rate are above 80%. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
